title: The treatment that wins twice and loses overall
statement: Two treatments, 350 patients each. Treatment $A$ cures $78\%$; treatment $B$ cures $83\%$. But split the patients into mild and severe cases and $A$ beats $B$ in both groups. Explain how that is possible.
solutionSteps: Here are the numbers. Mild cases: $A$ cures $81$ of $87$, $B$ cures $234$ of $270$. Severe cases: $A$ cures $192$ of $263$, $B$ cures $55$ of $80$.
Subgroup rates. Mild: $A = 81/87 \approx 93\%$ versus $B = 234/270 \approx 87\%$. Severe: $A = 192/263 \approx 73\%$ versus $B = 55/80 \approx 69\%$. $A$ wins both.
The reason is the mix, not the treatments. $B$ was given mostly mild cases ($270$ of $350$), which are easy to cure. $A$ was handed mostly severe ones ($263$ of $350$).
A pooled rate is a weighted average of the subgroup rates, and the weights differ between treatments. $B$'s average is pulled up by its easy caseload; $A$'s is dragged down by its hard one.

This is Simpson's paradox. Case severity is a lurking variable that drives both the assignment and the outcome, so pooling the groups compares different populations. The fix is to compare within strata — or randomise assignment so the mixes match.
